passage: Every morning in the village, Chaitanya, two, wanted the same faded blue shirt. When Pradeep held up a woollen cap for the chilly morning, Chaitanya pushed it away and clutched at his ears. "Itchy," he said. Pradeep felt the wool with his finger. "Scratchy, hmm." He offered a cotton scarf instead or the cap. Chaitanya chose the scarf and tugged it round his own neck.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya say about the woollen cap?
qa.a: He said, "Itchy."

qa.q: What might Chaitanya be feeling about the cap, and what else could explain his refusal?
qa.a: He probably felt the wool was uncomfortable on his skin. He might also just have wanted to decide for himself.

qa.q: What worked in Pradeep's approach?
qa.a: He checked the texture himself and gave a small choice, so Chaitanya kept his say and stayed warm enough. 🙂

qa.q: How might Pradeep see Chaitanya pushing the cap away?
qa.a: Pradeep seems to take it as a real comfort signal rather than naughtiness, since he feels the wool himself and offers a softer scarf.

grounding: A toddler insists on a favourite shirt and refuses a hat for sensory comfort, and small choices support autonomy.

passage: In a Lagos apartment, Ada, two, stood at the door in her socks and refused the sweater her mother held out. "No! Scratch!" Fatima turned the sweater inside out and found the stiff label at the collar. "That does scratch." She snipped it off, then offered two sweaters. "Green or yellow?" Ada took the yellow one and pulled it on herself, though the sleeve was half inside out.

qa.q: What did Fatima find at the collar of the sweater?
qa.a: She found a stiff label.

qa.q: What does Ada's no and scratch suggest, and what else might explain it?
qa.a: It suggests real discomfort from the label. It could also be that she wanted to choose for herself.

qa.q: What did Fatima do well?
qa.a: She checked for the cause instead of assuming defiance, removed the label and offered a choice.

qa.q: What would change if Fatima had insisted on the sweater as it was?
qa.a: Ada might have felt unheard and uncomfortable, and the morning might have turned into a fight.

grounding: A toddler refuses clothing for texture and control, and small choices support autonomy.

passage: I'm Avni, Baljeet's big sister. Every morning Nani pulls his woolly cap on, and every morning Baljeet pulls it off, scratching his forehead, and screams. Nani says he's being stubborn. But I saw the red lines on his forehead. So on Tuesday I gave him my soft cotton cap. He touched it, pulled it on himself and kept it on all the way to the bus stop.

qa.q: What did Avni give Baljeet on Tuesday?
qa.a: Her soft cotton cap.

qa.q: What was Baljeet likely feeling when he pulled off the woolly cap?
qa.a: He was uncomfortable, probably itchy, and upset, which is why he scratched and screamed.

qa.q: What did Avni notice that Nani didn't?
qa.a: The red lines on Baljeet's forehead, a sign the wool was irritating him.

qa.q: How does Nani see Baljeet pulling off the cap?
qa.a: Nani thinks he is being stubborn, not uncomfortable.

grounding: A sister notices her toddler brother refuses a woolly cap because it itches, not out of defiance.

passage:
Monday: Santosh screamed when Tushar held up the blue T-shirt. He pointed at the orange one. "That!" Tushar gave in.
Wednesday: the orange T-shirt was in the wash. Santosh screamed again. Tushar held up two others. "Green or yellow?"
The next Monday: Tushar held up the orange and the green. Santosh thought, chose green, and pulled it on himself.

qa.q: Which T-shirt did Santosh choose the next Monday?
qa.a: The green one.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling when he screamed on Wednesday?
qa.a: He was frustrated and upset that his favourite orange shirt was missing and he had no say.

qa.q: Which of Tushar's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Offering two shirts to choose from worked, because Santosh got a small choice and calmed down.

qa.q: How might Tushar feel the next Monday?
qa.a: He would likely feel relieved and pleased that dressing was easy. 🙂

grounding: Over a week a father learns to offer his toddler clothing choices, supporting autonomy instead of fighting.

passage:
In the Delhi flat, Zainab, the nanny, buttoned Sarika into her new frock for the party. Sarika tugged at the neck, whining, and tried to pull it off.
"Such a pretty frock," said a visiting aunty. "Don't be naughty."
Zainab ran a finger inside the collar. Scratchy lace, and a pink mark on Sarika's neck. She changed her into the soft cotton one. Sarika stopped whining and twirled.

qa.q: What did Zainab find inside the collar?
qa.a: Scratchy lace, and a pink mark on Sarika's neck.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling when she tugged at the neck and whined?
qa.a: She was uncomfortable and irritated by the scratchy lace, not being naughty.

qa.q: What did Zainab do that was wise?
qa.a: She checked the collar before deciding and changed Sarika into a soft frock.

qa.q: How does the visiting aunty see Sarika's tugging?
qa.a: The aunty sees it as naughtiness, not discomfort.

grounding: A nanny finds that a toddler's refusal of a frock is about scratchy lace, not defiance, and changes it.

passage:
“Not that one! Dino!” Darshan pulled at the green dinosaur shirt on the chair.
“It's in the wash pile,” said Deepak. “But it's clean enough. Fine, dino shirt.”
Then Mummy held out the woolly cap. “It's cold, Darshan.”
“No! No hat!” He pushed it off, rubbing his forehead.
“He's just being stubborn,” said Mummy.
“Maybe it's itchy,” said Deepak. He felt the wool. “Scratchy. What about your soft hood?”
Darshan pulled up the hood himself.

qa.q: What was on Darshan's favourite shirt?
qa.a: A dinosaur; it is the green dinosaur shirt.

qa.q: Why did Darshan push the woolly cap off?
qa.a: He likely found the wool scratchy and uncomfortable, as his rubbing his forehead suggests, and he also wanted some say in what he wore.

qa.q: Which choice by Deepak worked, and why?
qa.a: Feeling the wool and offering the soft hood instead, which respected Darshan's comfort and still kept him warm.

qa.q: How does Mummy see Darshan's refusal at first?
qa.a: She sees it as stubbornness.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler insisting on a favourite shirt and refusing a scratchy cap, asserting choice and sensory comfort rather than defiance.
